title: The Devil Tarot Card Meaning: Upright, Reversed & Love
description: The Devil upright: attachment, habits; reversed: breaking free or a private struggle. Love, work, advice and Waite's 1911 words. Ask your question.
image_alt: The Devil, 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith card: a horned figure with bat wings raises one hand above a black block; a man and a woman stand chained to a ring in front of it, against a black sky.
capsule: The Devil, card XV, points to attachment, temptation and habits that hold you tighter than you would like. Reversed, that grip loosens, or the struggle goes private. It is a card about restriction, not a threat: the chains in the picture are loose. As a yes or no answer, upright gives no: what binds you is still in place.

blocks.heading: What is on The Devil card?
paragraphs: A huge horned figure with bat wings sits above a dark block, one hand raised, the other holding a torch that points down. Waite names him "the Horned Goat of Mendes, with wings like those of a bat", standing on an altar; in his left hand is "a great flaming torch, inverted towards the earth", and a reversed pentagram marks the forehead (p. 128). The raised right hand, Waite writes, is the reverse of the blessing given by the Hierophant (p. 128).

In front of the altar is a ring, and two chains run from it to the necks of a man and a woman. Waite compares them to Adam and Eve after the Fall and adds: "Hereof is the chain and fatality of the material life" (p. 128). Both have small horns and tails; for Waite the tails "signify the animal nature, but there is human intelligence in the faces" (p. 128).
The most hopeful line comes next: the figure above them "is not to be their master for ever" (pp. 128–131).

On the 1909 card the whole background is black, XV is printed at the top, and the loops of chain around the two necks hang loose. The man's tail ends in a small flame. The horned figure fills the upper half of the card and is its largest shape.

blocks.heading: What did Waite write about The Devil?
paragraphs: In plain words, the first list is about force: heavy pressure, great effort, a push that seems settled in advance. Waite adds a qualifier that is easy to miss: what is settled in this way is not, for that reason, bad (pp. 285–286). The second list shrinks the scene to weakness, pettiness and blindness, a hold you cannot see clearly. Arcana Diary reads no fixed fate in this card or any other; the loose chains matter more.
Waite also recalls that older decks tied two small demons to the pedestal by a cord, and he praised Papus for replacing them with a man and a woman "yoked only to each other" (p. 25).

blocks.heading: What does The Devil mean upright?
paragraphs: Upright, The Devil points to attachment: a habit, a pattern, a craving or a dependence that has more say in your life than you would like. Temptation belongs here too, the pull toward what feels good now and costs you later.

The picture is the key to reading it calmly. The chains run to the necks of the two figures, yet the loops are loose, and nothing in the card says they cannot step out. The restriction is real, and it is not complete.
Naming what has a grip on you is where change starts. If this fits your situation, ask: what do I keep going back to even when part of me would rather not?

blocks.heading: What does The Devil mean reversed?
paragraphs: Reversed, The Devil often shows breaking free: a pattern losing its hold once you see it for what it is, a loosening grip on a habit you have outgrown. It can also point to a private struggle, a pull you would rather not look at and keep out of sight, even from yourself.
Waite's reversed list ends with blindness, which sits close to that second reading: a hold works best while it stays unseen. Reading this side as release is modern, not Waite's.
Either way, honesty helps. Admit the pull, then make one choice against it. If denial is part of the picture, start by simply noticing when the habit shows up.

blocks.heading: What does The Devil mean in love?
paragraphs: In love, The Devil asks where desire, habit or the fear of being alone may be limiting you. If you are single, it can point to a pattern you keep repeating: the same type of person, the same story, chosen because it is familiar rather than good for you.
In a relationship, it can describe an attachment that feels more like a chain than a choice, or a strong pull that crowds out other needs. It speaks about your own side of that pull.
Reversed in love, it can show an old pattern loosening. What would you choose if familiarity were not part of the decision?

blocks.heading: What does The Devil mean for work and money?
paragraphs: At work, The Devil can point to a job or routine you stay in only out of habit, overwork that has turned compulsive, or a tempting shortcut. The card asks what keeps you in place and whether that chain is really locked.
With money, look at your own patterns: is there a spending impulse that keeps coming back even though you would rather it did not?
Reversed, notice where you are already beginning to step out of an old routine.

blocks.heading: What is The Devil's advice?
paragraphs: Notice one habit that pulls at you and skip it once, on purpose. The advice here is to test the chain: it may lift more easily than you expect. Afterward, write down how it felt to choose differently.

blocks.heading: Is The Devil a yes or no card?
The Devil as a person and as a feeling
paragraphs: In a spread, The Devil may describe someone caught in a strong pull, or a dynamic built on dependence and temptation. When it points at you, it marks a part of you that is attached to something. What it names inside is craving, or the uneasy comfort of a familiar trap; reversed, relief starts to mix in as the hold eases.

pairs.text: A hold broken all at once. What kept you in place gets shaken loose.
Feeling trapped, twice over. Check which limits are real and which are only beliefs.
Temptation dressed up as choice. Go for the option that is real, not the one that glitters most.
Holding on hard. Ask whether you are protecting something or being held by it.

blocks.heading: The Devil or The Lovers?
paragraphs: Both cards show a man and a woman beneath a large figure. In The Lovers, Waite describes "a great winged figure with arms extended, pouring down influences" over "two human figures, male and female, unveiled before each other" (p. 92). The Devil keeps the pair but adds chains. The Lovers is a choice made freely, in line with your values; The Devil is a pull that keeps choosing for you.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask yourself about The Devil
paragraphs: Which habit has more power over my days than I would like?
If the chain is loose, what keeps me from lifting it off?
What would one small choice against this pull look like?

faq.q: Is The Devil a good or bad card?
faq.a: It is a demanding card, not a bad sign. It shows where something has power over you so you can see it plainly, and seeing it is what weakens that power. Nothing in it announces misfortune; it names a pull, not a punishment.

faq.q: Does The Devil card mean something evil?
faq.a: No. The name and the horned figure look alarming, but the card is about attachment and habit, not wickedness or danger. Even Waite remarked that in older decks the main figure "is not particularly evil" (p. 25), and in his own design the one who rules the chained pair does not rule them forever (pp. 128–131).

faq.q: Does The Devil always mean temptation?
faq.a: No. Temptation is one face of it, but the card covers any pull that narrows your freedom: a routine kept out of inertia, a fear that keeps you small, the need to be needed. Look for the spot in your question where something feels stuck, and start there.

faq.q: Why are the chains loose on The Devil card?
faq.a: Because the hold it shows is real but not final. On the 1909 card the rings of chain do not tighten around the throats; they could be lifted. Waite does not comment on this detail, so reading it as a possible way out is the modern view used on Arcana Diary.

waite.quote: Ravage, violence, vehemence, extraordinary efforts, force, fatality; that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil. Reversed: Evil fatality, weakness, pettiness, blindness.
